properties.statement:
`record_change` SILENTLY OVERWRITES THE `name` OF THE ChangeEvent IT IS FILED UNDER, SO THE TOOL WHOSE PURPOSE IS PRESERVING PRIOR STATE DESTROYS PRIOR STATE ONE NODE OVER. Found by doing it, 2026-08-15, while recording Alex's feedback — not by reading code, and not by any gate.

MEASURED. `add_change_event` created `chg:change-type-gap-corroborated-by-a-second-project` with a name explaining why `resync` was the least-wrong `change_type` for that edit. The next call was `record_change` with the same `change_event_id` and its own `name` describing the SNAPSHOT. The reply's `current` field came back holding the ChangeEvent with the snapshot's name, and `get_node` confirmed it: the event's original name was gone, with nothing said. The snapshot itself was correct — it captured the pre-edit statement, which is what it is for.

WHY IT IS EASY TO MISS: the call reports success, the snapshot is genuinely right, and the loss is in a DIFFERENT node from the one the caller is thinking about. Nothing in the reply says a property was replaced. The only reason it was caught here is that the overwritten text had just been written by hand in the previous call and was still in view.

WHAT `name` MEANS IN THAT CALL IS THE AMBIGUITY: `record_change`'s parameter list reads (epoch, change_event, name, target_type, target_id, change_type, action), and every other parameter describes THE CHANGE RECORD. Reading `name` as the record's name is the natural interpretation and it is the one the caller wants; the implementation applies it to the EVENT. Two different things want a name here and the API gives them one field.

SIBLING OF, AND SHARPER THAN, A REPORTED ONE. Alex's item 2 says the record-before-you-edit discipline loses to parallel tool calls: he snapshotted a Decision after a sibling call had already merged it, so the Snapshot stored the NEW statement. That is a caller-ordering hazard and his fix shape — refuse when the target's current hash is not what the caller thinks it is — addresses it. THIS ONE IS NOT AVOIDABLE BY ORDERING: the sequence here was strictly serial, one call at a time, exactly as the skill prescribes, and the loss happened anyway. Doing it right is not a defence.

WHAT IS ESTABLISHED: one serial reproduction, confirmed by get_node afterwards. WHAT IS NOT: whether the same overwrite hits other properties of the event, how many existing ChangeEvents in this graph already carry a snapshot's name instead of their own (cheap to sweep and not yet done), or whether any reader depends on the current behaviour.

FIX SHAPES, smallest first: leave the event's `name` alone when it already has one, and use the passed name for the Snapshot only; or split the parameter into `snapshot_name` so the two nameable things are distinguishable; or, at minimum, report in the reply that the event's name was replaced — this project's own rule is that nothing is silently dropped and partial-success fields are always present.
